statement: In healthy adults in sleep-laboratory studies, drinking alcohol in the hours before bed, compared with the same people on a night without alcohol, did not detectably shorten the time taken to fall asleep on average (2.0 minutes shorter, 95% CI 4.3 shorter to 0.2 longer), although in the dose analysis it was shorter after larger amounts, and evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes total sleep time (10.1 minutes less, 95% CI 24.6 less to 4.4 more; prediction interval 71.5 minutes less to 51.3 more), waking during the night or sleep efficiency, in a meta-analysis of 27 mostly crossover studies (Gardiner et al., 2025, journal pre-proof). In three of five studies people felt they fell asleep faster after alcohol. Most studies did not hold time in bed constant, and nearly all gave alcohol shortly before bed. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
plain: In sleep-lab studies, a drink before bed did not make people fall asleep faster on average, and its effect on how long they slept is unclear.
population: Healthy adults aged 18 to 70, mostly young, in 27 sleep-laboratory studies
exposure: A measured amount of alcohol drunk before bed, nearly always shortly before bedtime (study amounts and timings on the study card)
comparator: The same people on a night without alcohol (placebo or no alcohol)
outcome: Sleep onset latency, total sleep time, wake after sleep onset and sleep efficiency (polysomnography); perceived time to fall asleep
magnitude: Sleep onset latency -2.0 min (95% CI -4.3 to 0.2; prediction interval -11.6 to 7.5), k = 34, n = 271, p = 0.074; shorter with larger doses (p = 0.004), not moderated by timing (p = 0.684). Total sleep time -10.1 min (-24.6 to 4.4; prediction interval -71.5 to 51.3), k = 34, n = 284, p = 0.160, not moderated by dose (p = 0.701) or timing (p = 0.488). Wake after sleep onset +4.0 min (-2.3 to 10.3). Sleep efficiency -0.7% (-1.8 to 0.3). Perceived sleep onset shorter in 3 of 5 studies.

evidence.extracted: Sleep onset latency did not differ between alcohol and control (-2.0 min, 95% CI -4.3 to 0.2; prediction interval -11.6 to 7.5; k = 34, n = 271; p = 0.074); it was shorter after larger doses (meta-regression k = 30, n = 222; p = 0.004); timing did not moderate it (p = 0.684).

risk_of_bias.note: As for the REM claim: 11 of 27 studies at high risk of bias; time in bed often uncontrolled, which directly affects total sleep time.

inconsistency.note: Studies point both ways for total sleep time; this is reflected in the wide prediction interval and counted under imprecision rather than twice.

indirectness.note: Healthy adults drinking before bed; the laboratory timing is stated in the claim.

imprecision.note: The total-sleep interval includes both a loss of about 25 minutes and a gain; the prediction interval spans about two hours.

grade.reasoning: Controlled crossover experiments start high; downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision, giving low. The relation is insufficient evidence rather than no detectable change because the total-sleep and night-waking intervals do not exclude meaningful effects (METHODS §6.3); for sleep onset latency alone the interval excludes an average shortening of more than about 4 minutes, but the dose analysis shows shortening after larger amounts. Status mixed: individual studies found total sleep reduced (five) and increased (two).
